title: Ki Lo Na'eh
description: Ki Lo Na'eh ("For to Him it is fitting"), the Passover Seder hymn, in Hebrew to the traditional tune the Union Haggadah printed in 1923, in four parts of our own. Each verse praises Hashem as mighty, holy and strong in His kingship, and everyone answers: Yours, and Yours, Lord, is the kingdom, for to Him praise is fitting. The soprano sings the verses alone, as the print's solo, and everyone sings the chorus.

credits.words: traditional Hebrew hymn of the Passover Haggadah

licence.words: public domain: traditional, anonymous; already in the seder of Jacob ben Judah of London's Etz Hayyim, dated 1287 (David Kaufmann, Jewish Quarterly Review 4, 1892; the Encyclopaedia Judaica says about 1286), so older than the fifteenth century the Union Haggadah's notes give
licence.tune: public domain: traditional; in the Union Haggadah (1908), printed as 'Traditional' in its revised edition (1923)
licence.source: melody and words from The Union Haggadah: Home Service for the Passover, revised edition (edited and published by the Central Conference of American Rabbis, copyright 1923; the music 'as edited by the Society of American Cantors'), pp. 84 to 85, 'Ki Lo Noeh', 'Traditional', Chorus, Andante con moto, in C, 4/4 with an eighth-note pickup, voice and piano: the chorus 'Ki lo noeh, ki lo yoeh', then, repeated for each verse, a solo verse and the chorus 'L'cho ul'cho...'; the three verses it prints are sung here ('Addir bim'lucho', 'Kodosh bim'lucho', 'Takkif bim'lucho', the poem's stanzas 1, 7 and 8 of eight). Written here in D, a tone up, so the tune (C4 to C5 as printed, D4 to D5 here) sits in the soprano's range; the piano part used only to check the chords (no arranger is named). The soprano sings the solo verses alone and everyone sings the chorus, as printed. Checked against the first edition (Central Conference of American Rabbis, Cincinnati, copyright 1908), pp. 54 to 55, 'Ki Lo Noeh', the same tune in the same key with verse 1 only (archive.org/details/ccar1908union, leaves n52 and n53). The words are the print's, respelled from its Ashkenazi transliteration in modern Israeli pronunciation (the print's ' dropped where modern Hebrew sounds no vowel, as in 'bimlucha' and 'yomru'; where the print gives it a note, "g'-du-dov", "l'-cho", "t'-mi-mov", it is spelled e: 'ge-du-dav', 'le-cha', 'te-mi-mav'), syllable for syllable as the notes carry them, except 'ka-ha-la-cha', whose two printed sixteenths on 'ka-ha' are sung as a dotted pair, like 'a-dir bim-' (the repeated G merged, every pitch kept), so no two very quick syllables come together. Breaths written in for beginners: before each new line, the note before the print's eighth rest gives up a quarter of a beat; the last 'ya-e' holds to the end of the bar (the print's fermata). Read from the scan at archive.org/details/unionhaggadahhom00unse (leaves n103 and n104); divine names in substituted forms (Hillel, 2026-11-11), the forms customary when singing outside prayer: Adoshem, where the print has Adonoi.
